title: Waking up
hookLine: praise to Allah who gave us life after death, and to Him is the return (Bukhari)
tomorrow: Dadi's at the door with her cane, going out alone. what does she say?

cards: Phones have a sleep mode: screen dark, still running, waiting for a touch. The first words the Prophet ﷺ said on waking go much further than that.
In Sahih al-Bukhari: praise to Allah, who gave us life after He had given us death, and to Him is the return. Gave us death? Nobody died last night.
Everyone just slept. So why would a morning line call sleep a kind of dying?

teach.b: The answer is in the Qur'an itself. Surah az-Zumar says that God takes the souls at the time of their death, and takes the souls that have not died, in their sleep.

He keeps the ones whose death is decreed, and sends the others back, for a set term. Sleep, in that verse, is a small letting-go. Each night the soul is held, and each morning, for now, it's given back.
That's the puzzle solved, and the detail to tell a friend tonight: in this tradition, waking up is a small rehearsal of rising again.

teach.h: IN YOUR NAME I DIE AND LIVE.
teach.b: The same hadith gives the night its own line, said lying down: in Your name, O Allah, I die and I live. Put the two together and a day has a shape. Handed over at night; handed back in the morning.
The waking line's last word is nushur, the return, a word the Qur'an also uses for the raising of the dead. So a morning isn't only a new day.
It's a life given back without being asked for, before you've done a single thing to earn it.

how: Muslims say this line on waking, often before getting out of bed, and say 'in Your name, O Allah, I die and I live' when lying down to sleep.

o: a prayer said at a deathbed, for a peaceful passing
a call that wakes the neighborhood for dawn prayer
praise said on waking, for life given back after sleep

games.q: the night and the morning — tap the pairs.
p: in Your name I die and I live
souls taken in sleep, sent back

s: the waking line calls sleep a kind of death
the Qur'an says souls are taken in sleep and sent back (39:42).
the waking line is a sad prayer about dying
it's praise: life given back, every morning.
the night line and the morning line come from different collections
both are in the same hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari.

games.q: your little brother hears the waking line and gets scared: 'did i die last night?' what's the kind, true answer?
o: no. sleep is a little letting-go, and God gives the day back. that's why we say thanks.
yes, everyone dies every night; that's exactly what the words mean.
it's just old-fashioned wording; don't think about what it means.
games.why: the Qur'an calls sleep a taking of the soul that's sent back (39:42). the waking line is thanks, not a warning.

practice: If there's water near you, take one slow sip, the way you might first thing in the morning, and notice it reach you.

Then say, aloud or inside, the waking line or its meaning: praise to Allah, who gave us life after death, and to Him is the return. If you don't pray, simply notice that this morning was handed to you; you didn't make it.

wordCard.voice: Waking up: the first line of the day, praise for life given back after sleep, with the return to Him in its last word.

orig.note: Arabic: the return, the raising; the last word of the waking line.

carryVoice: For the morning: alive again, each day handed back to you, not earned by you. Waking, explained.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 6312 (the lines for lying down and waking, narrated by Hudhayfa)
